title: A chapter a day
hookLine: most Bible-reading habits are small: one chapter, same time, every day

cards: January first. A fresh start, and a big resolution: this is the year I read the whole Bible, cover to cover. You start at Genesis.
Creation, the flood, Abraham, Joseph: it moves. Exodus: plagues, the sea splitting.

Then you reach Leviticus, chapter after chapter of rules for sacrifices, offerings and purity, and somewhere in there the bookmark stops moving. There's an older way in, and it isn't a grand plan. It's small.
One chapter. Same time. Same chair.

teach.b: The idea is old. In the book of Acts, the people of a town called Berea are praised because they "searched the scriptures daily." Not in one heroic weekend.
God tells Joshua, "thou shalt meditate therein day and night."
A little, often. A chapter of a Gospel takes a few minutes to read, about as long as this lesson. Here's a surprise: chapter numbers aren't part of the original text.
The biblical writers didn't use them.
Chapter divisions were added many centuries later, and verse numbers later still. They're handles, and Christians have built all kinds of plans on them.
A Scottish minister, Robert Murray M'Cheyne, made a plan to take his congregation through the Bible in a year. The Book of Common Prayer takes Anglicans through the whole book of Psalms every month.

Catholics hear scripture in a set cycle of readings at Mass, and some Protestants use reading plans on their phones. If you're starting from nothing, a common piece of advice is: don't start at Genesis.
Start with a Gospel. Mark has sixteen chapters: sixteen days, and you've read a whole account of the life of Jesus. Missed a day?
The plan doesn't care. You pick it up where you left off.

how: Some Christians read a chapter or a set passage of the Bible every day, often with a reading plan, a daily devotional or the church's lectionary, at a regular time such as early morning or before bed.

games.why: a Gospel. Mark has sixteen chapters: sixteen days for a whole account of the life of Jesus.

practice: Picture your ordinary day and find a few minutes that are already yours, morning coffee, the bus, lunch, right before bed, and a place to match: a chair, a corner, a seat on the train.
See yourself there with a Bible, or an app, open to Mark, chapter one. If you pray, offer that time to God before it starts; if you don't, simply decide it's yours.

wordCard.voice: Capitulum, Latin for a little head, a heading, the root of the word chapter: a small, steady habit, one chapter at a time.

orig.note: Latin: a little head, a heading. where the English word chapter comes from.
